sources.title: Argentine Government, 135 Years of Law 1420
sources.note: 1884 law established common, free, compulsory, gradual primary education.

sources.title: National General Archive, Brooms and Roofs
sources.note: 1907 Buenos Aires tenement rent strike, women’s household labor, children and rooftop images.

sources.title: National Department of Labour, 1908 Tenant-Housing Report
sources.note: Contemporary report says tenant strikers demanded lower rent and better hygiene; tenement light, air and sanitary conditions were poor.

sources.title: Argentine Cultural Heritage Register, Mate
sources.note: Yerba mate has Guaraní roots; people share a gourd and bombilla in rounds, with one person preparing and serving, though customs vary.

sources.title: UNESCO, Tango
sources.note: Tango developed among urban lower classes in Buenos Aires and Montevideo through European, African-descended and criollo cultural exchange.

sources.title: Argentine National Migration Museum, Immigrants’ Hotel
sources.note: Early twentieth-century immigrant hotel offered arrivals accommodation, a bank, and medical care for travel-related illness and poor food.

sources.title: Argentine Government, Women’s Political Rights Became Law
sources.note: Women won national vote in 1947 after long organizing, and voted in a presidential election in 1951.

sources.title: Argentine Government, International Workers’ Day History
sources.note: Perón-era labor rights and 1949 constitutional recognition of work, health, social security and family protection.

sources.title: Argentine Government, 1930 Coup
sources.note: Military coup in 1930 interrupted constitutional politics.

sources.title: Casa Rosada Museum, The Radical Presidencies
sources.note: Yrigoyen presidencies followed 1916 electoral opening; political conflict, violence and 1930 end.

sources.title: Argentine Government, The 1955 Military Regime
sources.note: 1955 coup overthrew Perón and installed military rule, part of repeated alternation of elected and military governments.

sources.title: National Memory Archive, Argentina
sources.note: Archive preserves evidence of human-rights crimes in 1976–83 military dictatorship and reparations.

sources.title: Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo, Our History
sources.note: Grandmothers organized in 1977 to find children taken or born in captivity under state terror; identity includes family, language and community.

sources.title: Argentine National Electoral Directorate, 1983 Election
sources.note: 1983 election restored democratic civilian government after the 1976 military dictatorship.

sources.title: Argentine Government, 1994 Constitution Reform
sources.note: 1994 constitutional reform changed presidential term, judicial council and Buenos Aires autonomy.

sources.title: Argentine Government, Cecilia Grierson Historic Grave
sources.note: Cecilia Grierson graduated 1889 as first Argentine woman physician and worked for women’s civil and political rights.

sources.title: Argentine Government, Public Health Commemorative Banknote
sources.note: Grierson founded a nursing school; Ramón Carrillo expanded public health; their work is commemorated by the state.

sources.title: Nobel Prize, Bernardo Houssay Facts
sources.note: 1947 medicine prize for discovery of anterior pituitary hormone’s role in sugar metabolism.

sources.title: Argentine National Heritage, Wilde Sewage Pumping Station
sources.note: Buenos Aires hired John Bateman in 1871 and built water and sewage works; sewer plan accepted 1878 and plant construction began 1884.

sources.title: Argentine National Water and Sanitation Plan
sources.note: 1871 yellow-fever epidemic exposed unsafe water and waste; water and sewer works expanded slowly, not evenly nationwide.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Imported Argentina map coverage begins c. 1878; political independence dates to 1816. The imported polygon is not evidence that Indigenous lands were empty or correctly bounded.

Everyday examples are situated in Buenos Aires tenements, an immigrant hotel, cultural mate practice and specific scientific careers, not universal national conditions. Narrative awaits independent review.

proposedOverrides.summary: Argentina declared independence in 1816 and formed a federal constitutional republic in the nineteenth century. State campaigns from 1878 seized Indigenous lands; the map’s 1878 start is not the country’s beginning. Immigration, schools, tango, mate and science shaped daily life amid inequality. The dictatorship from 1976 to 1983 ended with a return to democracy; Argentina continues.

identityEvidence.assessment: Imported label confirmed; historic border accuracy and Indigenous sovereignty unverified.
